items.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Chromatin organization reflects the coordinated activities of histone modifications and chromatin-associated proteins. Inspired by single-cell genomics, we investigated whether genomic bins could be treated as multidimensional observations to identify biologically interpretable chromatin-associated signatures and characterize their genomic patterns across cell types. Methods: We integrated genome-wide profiles of CTCF occupancy and four histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K9ac, H3K27me3, and H3K9me3) at 1 kb resolution in HCT116 and K562 cells. Unsupervised dimensionality reduction and clustering were used to characterize chromatin-associated signatures. Principal component analysis (PCA) and integration with Hi-C data were used to examine differences between cell lines and associations with local genome architecture. Results: Five clusters of genomic bins were identified, characterized by H3K9me3-enriched, CTCF-enriched, acetylation-enriched, mixed repressive, and H3K27me3-enriched signatures. Among the selected features, H3K27me3 exhibited the greatest separation between HCT116 and K562 in the first two principal components, followed by CTCF. Integration with Hi-C data showed that CTCF-enriched regions were preferentially associated with previously annotated CTCF–CTCF chromatin loop anchors in both cell lines, consistent with the established architectural role of CTCF. Together, these findings highlight distinct chromatin-associated signatures and their relationships with higher-order genome architecture across the two cancer cell lines. Conclusions: Treating genomic bins as multidimensional observations provides a complementary exploratory approach for characterizing chromatin-associated signatures. Our findings illustrate its potential for comparing chromatin-feature organization between cell types and examining relationships with established features of three-dimensional (3D) genome architecture.</jats:p>
title: Integrating CTCF and Histone Modification Profiles Identifies Distinct Chromatin Signatures in Human Cancer Cell Lines
